title: Deployment venue selector — customer POC playbook and decision notebook
content:
Purpose and context:
This is a lightweight, repeatable playbook and decision notebook for deciding which deployment venue to recommend for a customer POC: Hosted API (fastest to ship), Dedicated (reserved capacity for predictable throughput), or Private (VPC/on-prem for sovereignty/compliance).

Audience:
- Solutions Engineering lead interacting with customer technical and security stakeholders
- Sales engineer bringing the POC up during the evaluation phase
- Eng stakeholders who will estimate capacity and cost for a follow-on purchase

High-level POC questions to answer (early):
1) What is the primary success metric for the POC? (latency percentile, token cost, throughput, functional accuracy, data residency)
2) Is customer data considered sensitive (PII, PHI, regulated financial records)?
3) What are the expected steady-state and peak qps? Expected average tokens per request?
4) Are there integration constraints (on-prem DB access, private networks, strict egress controls)?
5) Timeline and procurement constraints (need to be live in X weeks, or must pass infosec review first)?

Quick decision rubric (use as initial filter):
- If time-to-first-response <= 3 days and no special data residency: Hosted -> start there.
- If predictable throughput, SLA, or consistent latency >= requirement and customer is okay with reserved capex: Dedicated -> propose capacity commit.
- If regulated data, must not leave tenant network, or requires HSM/KMS under customer control: Private -> engage infra team and security.
- If mixed requirements: staged approach (hosted -> dedicated -> private) using canary bridge and data path proofs of concept.

POC design options (three canonical templates):
1) Hosted-first rapid validation
   - Objective: prove integration, prompt engineering, basic latency/cost profile, UX validation
   - Components: Redwood hosted API, short-lived API key, sandbox dataset (anonymized), simple routing from customer app to Redwood endpoint
   - Observability: Redwood Console dashboard (per-route latency and cost), lightweight eval harness (10–50 queries), manual QA script
   - Security: only test data, avoid PII; use encrypted storage for any logs; document deletion process
   - Expected timeline: 2–7 days
   - Typical risks: inference results are valid but not representative of private data distributions; security team may later block hosted usage

2) Dedicated/Reserved capacity validation
   - Objective: demonstrate sustained throughput, consistent p99 latency under planned load, cost predictability
   - Components: dedicated GPU pool configured for target qps, autoscaling floor/ceiling, capacity reservation aligned with expected concurrent requests
   - Observability: extended load test (1–2 hours ramp), token-level cost reports, tracing hooks to simulate real traffic patterns
   - Security: shared-network isolation by tenant, TLS, customer-managed auth layer optional
   - Expected timeline: 2–4 weeks (capacity provisioning + tuning)
   - Typical risks: commit sizing mismatch -> under/overprovision, procurement latency for reserved billing

3) Private deployment (VPC or on-prem)
   - Objective: meet compliance/data-sovereignty requirements, integrate with internal KMS/HSM, guarantee no egress to public cloud
   - Components: private control plane, private data path, optional offline model images, enterprise support bundle, audit logging
   - Observability: local telemetry collectors forwarded to customer SIEM, audit log export to customer KMS
   - Security: full-network isolation, HSM/KMS integrations, annual penetration test checklist
   - Expected timeline: 6–12 weeks (depends on customer infra, procurement, security signoff)
   - Typical risks: long procurement, infra compatibility, higher operational support burden

Decision factors and how to weigh them:
- Latency sensitivity: if p95/p99 latency budgets are tight (<200ms p95), prioritize regional dedicated placement or edge cachings (prefer dedicated or hosted regional with caching).
- Throughput and cost: if cost/throughput dominates (e.g., millions of tokens/day), run a cost simulation: hosted per-token vs dedicated hourly GPU amortization. Use Redwood Optimize recommendations to simulate.
- Data controls: any requirement to keep data in customer network -> default to private unless a hybrid approach is acceptable.
- Timeline pressure: if less than 2 weeks, hosted-only or hosted-proxy for feature gating.
- Security/compliance: if customer requires direct KMS/HSM or SOC2 Type II evidence in their environment, plan private.

Sample lightweight scoring sheet (use for customer workshop) — score 0–3 each, sum: higher = favor private/dedicated
- Data sensitivity: 0 (public) – 3 (regulated PII/PHI)
- Latency criticality: 0 (noninteractive) – 3 (sub-200ms p95 interactive)
- Throughput scale: 0 (sporadic) – 3 (high sustained throughput)
- Timeline urgency: 0 (6+ weeks ok) – 3 (must ship <2 weeks) [invert during tally]
- Procurement friction: 0 (no procurement) – 3 (requires contracting/enterprise procurement)

Testing and validation plan (POC checklist):
- Functional tests: baseline prompt set, edge-case prompt set, hallucination/consistency tests
- Performance tests: 1K-request ramp test, p50/p95/p99 measurements, cold-starts with KV-cache disabled/enabled
- Cost tests: token distribution analysis, simulated 30-day run cost using observed token sizes, compare hosted vs dedicated amortized cost figures
- Security tests: network egress verification, key rotation proof, confirm audit log retention policy
- Ops tests: failover scenarios, fallback model routing, canary rollback test

Customer workshop agenda (90 minutes) — use during intake call:
1) 10m: Goals and constraints framing (who owns success metrics)
2) 15m: Data sensitivity and integration checklist (network access, KMS, DBs)
3) 20m: Traffic profile walk-through (expected qps, token sizes, peak windows)
4) 20m: Tradeoffs + demo of a hosted quickpath vs dedicated sizing example (interactive)
5) 15m: Timeline + procurement constraints, agree next steps
6) 10m: Assign owners + immediate blockers

Example customer vignette (short):
Retail analytics startup: needs sub-300ms p95 for live chat recommendations, sensitive purchase history but anonymizable for POC, expects 300 reqs/min peak. Workshop outcome: start hosted regional with request-level anonymization and edge prefix caching, run a 2-week contractless proof; if 30-day sim shows >20% cost advantage for dedicated, propose a reserved pool sized for 4 GPUs with autoscale cap and 2-week canary transition path.

Unresolved questions to surface early (tickets to create):
- What is canonical anonymization pipeline for customer data? (JIRA-SE-4320)
- Does the customer require on-prem model artifacts or is network isolation sufficient? (CONFL-8019)
- Is there internal billing approval for a dedicated capacity commit? If >$X/month, escalate to enterprise sales.

Operational playbook snippets (notes for SEs):
- When proposing hosted for POC, always include a short-term data deletion SLA and an audit log capture for the customer security reviewer.
- For dedicated proposals, include a cost delta table (hosted vs reserved vs amortized on-prem) with assumptions documented in-line.
- For private, capture networking diagram early: exact CIDR blocks, required egress ports, and KMS endpoints.

Action items and owners (initial):
- Asha: build anonymization checklist and sample script (due 2025-03-05)
- Liam: prepare dedicated capacity sizing template + cost calculator (due 2025-03-07)
- Sofia: draft private deployment networking questionnaire for customers (due 2025-03-03)
- Devon: create load test harness for mixed token distributions (due 2025-03-10)

Appendix (quick links and templates):
- Sizing template: github.com/redwood-inference/templates/dedicated-sizing.xlsx
- Workshop slide deck: CONFL-7901 (SE playbook deck)
- POC intake form: CONFL-7892

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a 2-week "security-safe hosted bridge" where anonymized traffic runs in hosted while proving integration; document fallback to private if security team rejects hosted live data.
- Add a small set of canned anonymization functions we can drop into customer workspaces to reduce friction.

End of playbook.
